card.title: Back in Our Roles
card.instruction: Return immediately to the role you usually play in this relationship, even when the present situation calls for something different.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You're crying, love. I'll make tea and ring your manager, like last time.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Mum, I've been promoted. Could you just listen?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Of course. Will they give you enough staff?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Yes. Just raise your cup and say congratulations.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Congratulations. Now, who covers you when you're ill?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 resumes maternal crisis management, A3 turns promotion news into staffing worry, and A5 returns to protective contingency after the requested congratulations.

responseLogic.evidence: B2's promotion correction informs A3's staff question; B4's exact congratulation request is obeyed before A5 resumes illness coverage.

relationship.evidence: B2 wants the good news heard and B4 offers a simple way to celebrate it.

heightening.evidence: A5 uses B4's congratulation ritual briefly, then reveals that the habitual protector role immediately returns.

specificity.evidence: A1-B2 establish mother and adult child, with tears misread before the promotion is explained.

brevityWit.evidence: A5's coverage question is a specific return to the familiar role after the one-word celebration.

coach2.stated: B2 explicitly changes the meaning of the tears; A3-A5 accept the promotion but respond through habitual concern.
coach2.inferred: B2 names Mum and identifies the changed occasion as good professional news.
coach2.missing: No essential missing fact about the previous manager incident is needed.
coach2.firstDefect: No mandatory defect; the role persists even after A briefly attempts the requested celebration.

A3-B4.evidence: B4 confirms adequate staff and requests a congratulatory toast.
